front: Distributed File Systems: what is a DFS?
back: An environment that involves multiple machines for the delivery of the filesystem service. The OS can hide the fact that there is no local physical storage; files are maintained on a remote filesystem accessed over the network.

front: DFS: why does the OS export a high-level filesystem interface?
back: To abstract the (potentially) different types of storage devices on a machine and unify them under a common API, hiding even the fact that storage may be remote rather than local.

front: DFS models: what is the simple model?
back: Clients being served files from a server running on a different machine.

front: DFS models: a server distributed across multiple machines can arrange files in which two ways?
back:
• Replicated: files replicated across every machine
  • Partitioned: files split so each machine holds a subset

front: DFS models: what is a peer-based model?
back: Files are stored on and served from all machines, blurring the line between servers and clients. Every node is a peer responsible for maintaining files and providing the service, each handling some portion of the load (often requests for files local to it).

front: Remote file service extremes: describe the upload/download model.
back: When a client wants a file it downloads the entire file, performs modifications locally, then uploads the entire file back to the server. This is less like a proper filesystem and more like FTP servers or version management systems such as SVN servers.

front: Remote file service extremes: benefit of the upload/download model?
back: All modifications are done locally, so they can be done quickly without incurring any network cost.

front: Remote file service extremes: two downsides of the upload/download model?
back:
• Client must download the entire file even for small modifications
  • It takes file access control away from the server: once given out, the server has no idea what the client is doing with the file or when it will give it back; this makes some file-sharing operations difficult to execute

front: Remote file service extremes: describe the true remote file access model.
back: The file stays on the server and every single operation passes through the server; the client makes no attempt at local caching or buffering.

front: Remote file service extremes: benefit of true remote file access?
back: The server has full control and knowledge of how clients access and modify a file, making it easier to keep the filesystem state consistent.

front: Remote file service extremes: two downsides of true remote file access?
back:
• Every file operation pays a network cost, even repeated reads of a read-only file, since local caching is bypassed
  • Limited scalability: the server overloads quickly and services fewer clients

front: Remote file service compromise: what does it let clients do?
back: Use their local memory/disk to store at least part of the file being accessed, including downloading blocks they are accessing and prefetching blocks they may soon access.

front: Remote file service compromise: two benefits of serving from a local cache?
back:
• Lower latency on file operations, since no extra network cost is incurred
  • Increased server scalability, since local service decreases server load

front: Remote file service compromise: once clients cache file portions, what two interactions with the server become necessary?
back:
• Notify the server of any modifications they make
  • Query the server at some reasonable frequency to detect whether cached files were changed by someone else

front: Remote file service compromise: what is the main downside?
back: The server becomes more complex: it must perform extra tasks and maintain extra state to provide consistency guarantees, and clients must understand file sharing semantics different from a normal local filesystem.

front: Remote file service compromise: what does the compromise preserve for the server, compared with upload/download?
back: The server keeps insight into what clients are doing and some control over which accesses are permitted, which makes consistency easier, while staying out of the way enough that some operations happen on the client, reducing load.

front: Stateless server: what does it keep, and what are the consequences for self-containment?
back: It keeps no state (no notion of which files/blocks are accessed, which operations are performed, or how many clients access how many files). As a result every request must be completely self-contained, so more bits go on the wire per request.

front: Stateless server: what must every self-contained request carry?
back:
• The file being accessed
  • The absolute offset within that file
  • Any data that needs to be written

front: Stateless server: which models can it support, and which can it not?
back: Suitable for the extreme models, but cannot be used for any model that relies on caching: without state you cannot achieve consistency management.

front: Stateless server: two positives?
back:
• No CPU/memory utilization needed to manage state
  • Very resilient: since requests rely on no internal state, a failed server simply needs to be restarted; clients reissue any requests that timed out and get the same answers they would have received anyway, and neither side needs to do anything else special to recover

front: Stateful server: what kinds of information does it maintain?
back:
• The clients in the system
  • Which files are being accessed
  • Which types of accesses are performed
  • Which clients have a file cached
  • Which clients have read/written the file

front: Stateful server: what capabilities does its state enable?
back: Caching with consistency guarantees, locking, and relative block requests ("next kB of data") instead of absolute offsets, since accesses are known.

front: Stateful server: what happens on failure, and what does that require?
back: All state must be recovered so the filesystem stays consistent. That requires more complex mechanisms: the state must be checkpointed so it can be rebuilt to represent what the clients were doing before the failure. There are also runtime overheads on the server to maintain state and execute the consistency protocols; how large depends on how caching is enabled and on the consistency requirements.

front: Caching state in a DFS: what does it allow clients to do?
back: Locally maintain a portion of the state (e.g. a file block) and perform operations on that cached state: open/read/write, etc.

front: Caching state in a DFS: what is required to keep cached portions consistent with the server's copy?
back: Cache coherence mechanisms.

front: Caching state in a DFS: what is the core coherence problem with two clients caching the same file portion?
back: If one client modifies its local portion and sends the update to the server, there must be a mechanism to make the other client aware of those changes.

front: Caching state in a DFS: in what ways can coherence mechanisms be triggered, and who can drive them?
back: Triggered on demand (on any file access), periodically, or on file open. They may be driven by either the client or the server.

front: Caching state in a DFS: why not do what shared memory multiprocessors do and propagate every write to every client caching the file?
back: It may not be realistic, given the much higher communication costs and latencies of distributed systems, and it may not even be necessary, given the ways files are actually shared.

front: Caching state in a DFS: what is the difference between a client-driven and a server-driven coherence mechanism?
back:
• Client-driven: the client asks whether the file has been updated
  • Server-driven: the server notifies the clients that have cached the file that their cached state has changed

front: File Caching Quiz: in a DFS with a single file server and many clients, where can files or file blocks be cached?
back:
• In client memory, in the client's buffer cache
  • On the client's local storage (hard disks, SSDs), which may be faster than going over the network
  • On the server, in the file server's buffer cache in memory

front: File Caching Quiz: when may caching in the file server's buffer cache not be very useful?
back: When many clients access the server at the same time with high request interleaving: there may be little locality among the accesses from many clients.

front: File sharing semantics: on a single-node UNIX system, when a process modifies a file, when do other processes see it and why?
back: Immediately, even if the change is not pushed to disk, because both processes have access to the same buffer cache.

front: File sharing semantics in a DFS: why can't we guarantee no staleness even if writes are pushed to the server immediately?
back: It takes time for an update to be delivered, so another client may keep reading stale data for a while. Because message latencies vary, there is no way to know how long to delay a read to ensure any write from anywhere in the system has arrived.

front: File sharing semantics in a DFS: what does a DFS typically sacrifice to maintain acceptable performance?
back: Some of the consistency; it accepts more relaxed file sharing semantics.

front: Session semantics: what happens on close and on open?
back: On close the client writes back whatever data was modified. On open the cache is skipped and the client checks the file server for a more recent version. The period between open and close is one session.

front: Session semantics: what consistency do you get, and what is the catch?
back: You can be reading a stale version while the file is open, but you are guaranteed consistent with the rest of the filesystem at the moment you open or close the file.

front: Session semantics: why are they poor for concurrent sharing?
back: For two clients to see each other's updates they must constantly close and re-open the file, and files that stay open for long periods may become severely inconsistent.

front: Periodic updates: how do client and server bound inconsistency?
back: The client writes back changes periodically; the server sends invalidation notifications periodically to enforce time bounds on inconsistency. On receiving a notification, a client must sync with the most recent version.

front: Periodic updates: how can the client's periodic write-back be thought of, and how does it differ from a lock?
back: As a lease on how long the client can use the cached data. It is not an exclusive lease like a lock; locking is a separate issue.

front: Periodic updates: besides limiting staleness, what does bounding the inconsistency buy?
back: Fewer conflicts accumulate between updates, so any conflicts are easier to correct.

front: Periodic updates: what explicit operations can the filesystem provide?
back: flush to push the client's updates to the server, and sync to sync the client's state with the remote server. They exist because the client does not know the start and end times of the synchronization periods. They are not DFS-specific; local filesystems use them too.

front: File sharing semantics: describe the immutable-files and transactions strategies.
back:
• Immutable files: you never modify an old file; you either delete it or create a new file with a new name
  • Transactions: the filesystem exports an API to group file updates into a single batch applied atomically

front: Immutable files: what real-world example does the lecture give?
back: Sharing photos via Instagram or Facebook: to change a photo, you upload the modified photo rather than editing the uploaded one.

front: DFS Data Structure Quiz: with a server-driven mechanism and session semantics, which per-file structures should the server keep: readers, current writer, current writers, version number?
back: Readers, current writers (plural), and version number; not "current writer". Server-driven means the server pushes invalidations to the clients, so it must know who has the file.

front: DFS Data Structure Quiz: why can session semantics have multiple current writers rather than one?
back: Changes become visible only when a session closes and a subsequent client opens the file, so overlapping sessions can see different versions of the file and write concurrently.

front: Session semantics: what happens when multiple concurrent writers all close the file?
back: Session semantics does not specify it: one version may become the valid one, the versions may be merged, or an error may be raised to the clients so they can resolve the conflict.

front: DFS Data Structure Quiz: what is the per-file version number for?
back: It lets clients know which version they were given, and lets the server tell which clients have been modifying an old version of the file versus the newest one.

front: File vs. directory service: which workload properties should be understood before choosing file sharing semantics, and what is the design goal?
back:
• Sharing frequency
  • Write frequency
  • How important a consistent view is for that type of file
Then design the filesystem to optimize for the common case.

front: File vs. directory service: why use different semantics for files and directories?
back: Regular files and directories often have very different access patterns, so it is common to treat them differently: one type of semantics for regular files and another for directories. Or, with periodic updates for both, less frequent write-backs for regular files than for directories, since directories are more frequently shared than the individual files in them.

text: Regular files and directories often have very different access patterns in terms of {{c1::locality}}, {{c2::lifetime of the files}}, {{c3::size distribution}}, and {{c4::how frequently they are accessed}}.

front: File vs. directory service: the lecture suggests less frequent write-backs for regular files than for directories. What does NFS do instead, and why?
back: The opposite: NFS checks directories less often than regular files, on the rationale that directories are modified less frequently.

front: Replication: three benefits of replicating the filesystem onto multiple machines?
back:
• Client requests can be load balanced across all machines, improving performance
  • The system is more available
  • More fault tolerant: when one replica fails, others serve clients with no degradation

front: Replication: why do writes become more complex, and what are two solutions?
back: A write must reach all replicas. Options: force clients to write synchronously to all replicas, returning only once every replica is updated (which slows down all writes), or write to one replica and have a background job asynchronously propagate the write to the others.

front: Replication: how are out-of-sync replicas reconciled?
back: They must be reconciled; one simple technique is voting, where the majority wins.

front: Partitioning: on what basis may files be partitioned?
back:
• Filename (e.g. files a to m on one machine, n to z on another)
  • Directory (partitioning the hierarchical namespace of the directory tree)
  • Other criteria

front: Partitioning: main benefit over replication regarding filesystem growth?
back: Better scalability: adding more machines means more files can be supported, whereas adding machines in the replicated approach does not let you support a larger filesystem.

front: Partitioning: why does it achieve greater availability than a single-server design?
back: Each server holds fewer files, so it can respond to requests for those files more quickly.

front: Partitioning: why are writes simple?
back: A single file lives on a single machine, so writes to that file are localized to that machine.

front: Partitioning: two downsides?
back:
• When a partition goes down, the data on it can no longer be accessed
  • Balancing is harder, and frequently accessed files can create hotspots

front: Replication and partitioning: what is the combined solution?
back: Partition the filesystem across some axis, then replicate each partition some number of times. Many big data filesystems used by companies like Google and Facebook take this approach.

front: Replication and partitioning: in the combined design, must every partition be replicated the same number of times?
back: No, the degree of replication can differ per partition. For example, partitions of read-only files can be replicated more than partitions of files that are also written.

front: Replication and partitioning: how can partition sizes and replication degrees be chosen to balance load?
back: Put frequently accessed files in smaller partitions and less frequently accessed files in larger ones, with different degrees of replication for each, so each machine receives about the same number of expected client requests.

front: Replication vs. Partitioning Quiz: three machines hold 100 files each. Total files stored, and percentage of files lost if one machine fails, for replicated vs. partitioned?
back:
• Replicated: 100 files total; 0% lost (two machines still hold all files)
  • Partitioned: 300 files total; 33% lost (every file on the failed machine)
Partitioning gives greater scalability, replication greater fault tolerance, so a mixed approach gives flexibility in achieving both size and resiliency.

front: NFS design: trace the path of a client file request through the layers.
back: The client uses the VFS with the same file descriptors/operations as local files. The VFS decides whether the file is local or must be pushed to the NFS client, which interacts with the NFS server via RPC. The server forms a proper filesystem operation delivered to its local VFS, then to the local filesystem interface.

front: NFS design: on the server machine, how do requests from the NFS server look?
back: Identical to filesystem requests coming from any other application running on the server machine.

front: NFS design: what is created on an open request, what does it contain, and when does it go stale?
back: The server creates a file handle, a byte sequence encoding information about the server machine and the file. It is returned to the client, maintained by the NFS client, and passed internally with every request for the file. It becomes stale if the file is deleted or the server machine dies; using a stale handle results in an error.

front: NFS design: how is file data carried on a write and on a read?
back:
• write: the data to be written is carried as part of the RPC request from client to server
  • read: the data blocks read are the results of the RPC request, passed back to the NFS client and then to the application

front: NFS File Handle Quiz: a handle becomes stale. Does that mean the file is outdated, the server is not responding, the file on the server was removed, or the file was open too long?
back:
Only the file on the remote server was removed.
  • Outdated file: may be a consistency problem, but it does not produce a stale handle
  • Server not responding: an RPC layer (possibly network) error, unrelated to the handle
  • Open too long: some DFSs limit how long a file stays open, but NFS does not

text: NFSv3 is {{c1::stateless}}, whereas NFSv4 is {{c2::stateful}}, so NFSv4 can support operations like file caching and file locking.
extra: Even though NFSv3 is stateless, the implementation typically includes modules that provide certain stateful functionality.

front: NFS versions: what semantics does NFS use for files that are not accessed concurrently?
back: Session semantics: on close all changes are flushed to the server, and on open a check is performed and cached portions are updated if necessary.

front: NFS versions: what do periodic updates do to session semantics?
back: They break session semantics when multiple clients are concurrently updating a file.

front: NFS versions: what are the default periodic-update periods for files and directories, and why?
back: The periods are configurable (periodic updates can even be disabled). By default: 3 seconds for files and 30 seconds for directories. Directories are modified less frequently, and when modified the changes are more easily resolved.

front: NFS versions: what is the NFSv4 delegation mechanism?
back: The server delegates to the client all rights to manage a file for a given period of time, which avoids the periodic update checks.

front: NFS versions: how does NFS lease-based locking work?
back: When a client acquires a lock the server assigns a time period during which the lock is valid. The client must either release the lock within that time frame or explicitly extend it.

front: NFS locking: what happens if a client holding a lock lease fails or loses connectivity?
back: The server sees the lease has expired and can assign the lock to another client. When the client comes back (or connectivity is re-established), it knows its lease expired and it no longer holds a valid lock, so it has to redo whatever changes it was trying to make.

front: NFS versions: what reader/writer lock does NFSv4 support?
back: "Share reservation", with mechanisms for upgrading from reader to writer and vice versa.

front: NFS Cache Consistency Quiz: which file sharing semantics does NFS support by default: UNIX, session, periodic, immutable, or neither?
back:
Neither.
  • Not immutable: NFS allows files to be modified
  • Not UNIX: updates are not guaranteed to be immediately visible
  • Not purely session: it can periodically check for intermediate updates during a session
  • Not purely periodic: changes still propagate on close and are checked on open

front: NFS: under what configuration does NFS behave with session semantics?
back: When the (configurable) periodic update checks are disabled. Otherwise it has both session-like and periodic-like elements.

front: Sprite DFS: how does Sprite differ from NFS, and how were its design decisions justified?
back: Sprite was a research DFS rather than a production one, but it was built and deployed at UC Berkeley and people used it. The authors used trace data from users of a real distributed filesystem to understand file access patterns and justify the design.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture uses Sprite only for cache consistency. What is the paper's other contribution that the lecture does not cover?
back: That Sprite's caches vary in size dynamically: the file system and virtual memory system each manage a pool of physical pages and negotiate over memory by comparing the ages of their oldest pages, so the file cache can grow to occupy most of a client's memory when VM does not need it (Sections 1 and 6).

front: Sprite paper: the lecture frames Sprite around consistency; what are the paper's headline results, which are actually about caching performance?
back: Client caches let diskless workstations run within 0-12% of workstations with local disks, cut server load by a factor of two or more, and cut network traffic by about a factor of four.

front: Sprite access-pattern analysis: what did the authors study?
back: How files are accessed in the production filesystem used by their department.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture says the access-pattern numbers come from a study of the authors' own filesystem. What does the paper say they actually came from?
back: The "BSD study" (Section 3): a separate trace-driven analysis of three time-shared VAX-11/780s running 4.2 BSD UNIX. Sprite's designers reused that trace rather than tracing Sprite itself; a measurement of Sprite's own production access came later (Baker et al., SOSP 1991).

front: Sprite paper: for what two purposes does the paper use the BSD trace?
back:
• A simulation (Tables 1 and 2) feeding each timesharing user into a simulated client, to estimate cache-consistency overhead
  • Section 7: estimating per-user I/O rates for sizing a Sprite server

front: Sprite access-pattern analysis: what fraction of file accesses are writes, and what does that imply for caching?
back: 33% of accesses are writes, so 66% of operations can be improved by caching. To leverage the cache for writes as well, a write-through policy is not sufficient.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture reads the one-third-writes figure as "66% of operations can be improved." How does the paper actually frame that limit?
back: As an upper bound: because about a third of accesses are writes, a caching scheme based on write-through "cannot reduce disk or server traffic by more than two-thirds" (Section 4.3). The two-thirds is a ceiling on savings, not a count of operations definitely improved.

front: Sprite access-pattern analysis: what open-duration statistics made session semantics' overheads too high?
back: 75% of files were open less than 0.5 seconds and 90% were open less than 10 seconds.

front: Sprite access-pattern analysis: what deletion statistics, plus rare sharing, led the authors to drop write-back-on-close?
back: 20-30% of new data was deleted within 30 seconds and 50% within 5 minutes, and file sharing was rare. So write-back on close was not really necessary.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture lumps "file sharing is rare" in with the deletion/open-duration trace numbers. How does the paper treat sharing differently?
back: "Rare" sharing is the paper's expectation about Sprite's own write-sharing, used to justify optimizing the consistency algorithm for the no-sharing case (Section 5); the paper does not list sharing frequency among the BSD study's access statistics in Section 4.3. Its own write-sharing evidence is the Section 5.3 simulation: 4041 blocks written through for concurrent write-sharing, 6887 flushed for sequential, and consistency was about one-fourth of server traffic.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture says the deletion statistics justified dropping write-on-close. Which statistic does the paper use to reject write-on-close, and what do the deletion statistics motivate?
back: The paper rejects write-on-close using the open-duration numbers (75% open under 0.5 s, 90% under 10 s; Section 4.3). The deletion statistics (20-30% of new data dies within 30 s, 50% within 5 min) motivate delayed writes in general: a policy that delays writes several minutes can substantially reduce traffic.

front: Sprite access-pattern analysis: sharing was rare, so did Sprite drop support for concurrent access?
back: No. It still had to support concurrent access; it just did not optimize for it.

front: Sprite from analysis to design: what caching and write policy did Sprite adopt?
back: Caching with a write-back policy to send changes to the server.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: describe the 30-second write-back rule.
back: Every 30 seconds a client writes back all blocks that have not been modified within the last 30 seconds. A file may be opened and closed multiple times by the client before any data is sent to the server.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: does Sprite write back on close, and what follows?
back: No. A client may finish with a file and close it while modified blocks remain in its cache. This is one way Sprite optimizes the 33% of accesses that are writes.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: what is the intuition behind writing back only blocks untouched for 30 seconds?
back: Blocks modified more recently will likely continue to be modified; it makes no sense to force write-backs on blocks that are likely to be worked on more. This avoids sending the same blocks to the server over and over.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: according to the lecture, which access-pattern observation is the 30-second write-back threshold related to?
back: The observation that 20-30% of new data was deleted within 30 seconds.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite paper: the lecture ties the 30-second write-back interval to the 30-second deletion figure. What does the paper actually say about where the 30 seconds comes from?
back: The paper does not derive it from the deletion figure. It adopts a UNIX-like delayed-write policy (every 30 seconds, dirty blocks not modified in the last 30 seconds are written back), which is the UNIX convention (the 30-second sync interval). The deletion stats argue for a longer delay (several minutes), not for 30 specifically, and the paper planned to experiment with longer intervals.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: how long does a block take to reach the server cache and the disk?
back: Per the paper (Nelson et al., Section 4.3): a block written on a client reaches the server's cache in 30-60 seconds and the disk 30-60 seconds after that.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: when a client opens a file being written by another client, what does the server do?
back: The server contacts the writer and collects all of the outstanding dirty blocks.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: why can directories not be cached on the client?
back: Every open operation has to go to the server, so directory-related operations such as looking up, opening, or creating a file cannot be performed using the client cache alone.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite paper: the lecture presents "every open goes to the server" as a mere consequence of write-back. How does the paper characterize this choice and its cost?
back: It is a deliberate design choice with a known cost: the algorithm depends on the server being notified of every open/close to detect concurrent write-sharing, which prohibits optimizations like name caching that let clients open files without contacting the server (Section 5). Andrew made the opposite choice, using server callbacks so clients can open cached files without contacting the server.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite paper: what does the paper estimate Andrew-style name caching and callback would buy Sprite (Table 8)?
back: Only a few percent in client-visible speed, but up to one-third less server and network utilization, potentially letting one server support 50% more clients.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite from analysis to design: what happens to caching on concurrent writes, and why is the cost acceptable?
back: Caching is completely disabled; all writes are serialized on the server side. Because concurrent writes do not happen frequently, this cost is not significant.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: Sprite paper: the lecture says concurrent write-sharing simply disables caching. What two actions does the paper say the server takes when it detects concurrent write-sharing at open?
back: (Section 5.1) (1) It tells the one client that has the file open for writing, if any (there can be at most one), to write all its dirty blocks back. (2) It tells all clients that currently have the file open that the file is no longer cacheable, so they drop its blocks and send future accesses to the server. Clients that do not have the file open but hold stale blocks are not notified; they take consistency actions on their next open. Disabling is per file and only while sharing is concurrent.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

text: Sprite distinguishes two situations: with {{c1::sequential write sharing}} (clients take turns writing over time) it allows caching and provides {{c2::sequential}} semantics; with {{c3::concurrent write sharing}} it {{c4::completely disables caching}} for that file.
extra: Dynamically enabling and disabling caching this way is one unique feature of Sprite.
source: Sprite DFS from Analysis to Design

front: File access in Sprite: in the multiple-readers-one-writer scenario, which operations go to the server and what must the writer track?
back: All open operations go through the server. All clients may cache blocks; the writer must also keep timestamps on each modified block to enforce the 30-second write-back policy.

front: File access in Sprite: after a writer closes, where are the contents, and what keeps server and client in sync?
back: The contents stay in the writer's cache; the next open still goes through the server. The server and client keep a version number to stay in sync.

front: File access in Sprite: what does the client track per file?
back:
• cache (overall yes/no)
  • cached blocks
  • timer for each dirty block
  • version number

front: File access in Sprite: what does the server track per file?
back:
• readers
  • writer
  • version

front: File access in Sprite: what is a sequential writer, and what does the server do when one arrives?
back: A new writer that comes along after the first writer has closed the file. The server contacts the old writer to gather all dirty blocks (convenient since the client tracks them), updates the stored writer to point to the new writer, and the new writer can proceed and cache the file.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture handles sequential write-sharing by "contacting the old writer to gather dirty blocks." What two separate problems and mechanisms does the paper distinguish (Section 5.2)?
back: (1) The opening client may hold out-of-date blocks in its own cache, solved by version numbers: the server increments a per-file version each time it is opened for writing, and a client flushes its cached copy on open if its version differs. (2) Current data may still sit in another client's cache since the last writer need not flush on close, solved by the server tracking the last writer and telling it to flush before the new opener reads. The lecture's "gather dirty blocks" is only the second mechanism.

front: File access in Sprite: what happens on concurrent sharing (a third writer wanting to write with the current writer)?
back: The server contacts the current writer to gather dirty blocks. Realizing that writer has not closed the file, the current writer writes back all of its dirty blocks and the server marks the file not cacheable, disabling caching of the file for everybody. Both writers keep access, but all operations go through the server.

front: File access in Sprite: what flag does the server maintain to control caching, and when is a file made cacheable again?
back: A cacheable flag on a per-file basis. When a writer closes a file the server sees it (every operation goes through the server) and makes the file cacheable again; the remaining clients can then start caching the file again.

front: Sprite paper: the lecture says that when a writer closes a concurrently shared file, the server makes it cacheable again and the remaining clients resume caching. What does the paper say?
back: The paper contradicts this. A non-cacheable file becomes cacheable again once it is no longer undergoing concurrent write sharing, but for simplicity Sprite does not re-enable caching for files that are already open (Section 5.1). The remaining writer still has the file open, so it would not resume caching until it closes and reopens the file; caching is re-enabled only for later opens.
